answerGuide: First response time shows speed to acknowledge; time to resolution shows speed to fix; CSAT shows customer feeling; first contact resolution and reopen rate show quality; backlog age shows risk.
Gaming risks: a quick useless reply lowers response time, closing tickets early lowers resolution time, surveying only happy customers inflates CSAT.
Read metrics together and sample real tickets.
Connect to your work: ticket inflow fell 35 percent after the documentation rewrite, and you checked which categories moved.
pitfalls: Naming one metric as the truth.
Taking credit for a trend without checking other causes.
followUps: Which metric would you watch if you could pick one?
How would you improve CSAT?
What would you do about a spike in reopened tickets?

prompt: A user says a page will not load shifts. What basic checks do you do in the browser before you escalate?
variants: How comfortable are you with browser developer tools and logs?
intent: Probes honest, practical troubleshooting depth for application support: you do not need to code, but you should gather real evidence.
answerGuide: Reproduce on your side with the same account type if possible, check a different browser, and clear obvious variables (cache, extension).
Open the browser developer tools: look at console errors and the network tab for failing requests, their status codes and timing.
Capture a screenshot and the request details for the ticket.
State your level: you read errors and status codes to describe the symptom; you do not debug code, so you pass precise evidence to engineers.
pitfalls: Claiming you can diagnose server code.
Escalating with no evidence at all.
followUps: What does a 500 mean versus a 403?
What would you do if only one customer has the problem?
How do you ask a customer to gather this safely?

prompt: You logged cases in Salesforce. What did a good case record contain?
variants: How did you document customer contacts?
intent: Verifies the earlier support job with specifics of case discipline, which also predicts note quality in any ticketing tool.
answerGuide: Contact and account, a short summary in the customer's words, product and version, steps taken, result, and the next action with a date.
Status updated at each contact, categorised consistently so reports mean something.
Notes written so someone else could pick up the case cold.
Be honest that it was phone and email support for an education publisher's software in 2021, and that you used Salesforce as a user, not an administrator.
pitfalls: Describing features you did not use.
Saying you wrote 'brief' notes with no standard.
followUps: How did you categorise cases?
What happened when a case went stale?
What carried over to later ticket work?

prompt: Do you use canned replies? How do you keep them from sounding robotic?
variants: How do you write the same answer many times well?
intent: Tests the balance of efficiency and personal tone in a high-volume support or customer success inbox.
answerGuide: Use templates for steps and policy wording, and personalise the opening (their issue, their name, their context) and the close.
Keep them in a shared library with an owner and review dates so they do not go stale.
Never paste a template that does not answer the question asked.
Spot repeated templates as a signal to fix the product or the knowledge base.
pitfalls: Sending a template that misses the point.
followUps: How do you decide when to write from scratch?
What does a repeat question tell you?
How do you handle tone in text only?

prompt: Exercise: a pharmacy manager writes, 'Three shifts I posted yesterday vanished from the list and I'm furious, I need coverage tonight.' Draft your reply and say what you do in parallel.
variants: Write a first response to an angry customer with an urgent problem.
intent: A timed writing task for support and customer success: graders read for empathy that is specific, a concrete next step, honesty about what is not yet known, and urgency handling.
answerGuide: Open by acknowledging the specific impact (coverage tonight) without blame or boilerplate.
Give an immediate workaround if one exists (how to check shift status, how to repost) and say what you are checking now.
State the next update time rather than promising a fix time you do not control.
In parallel: check whether the shifts were cancelled or filtered, look at recent changes, raise it to the on-call person with ids and times, and keep the thread updated.
pitfalls: Apologising at length and saying nothing.
Promising a fix time you cannot guarantee.
followUps: What would you do if the shifts were cancelled by someone else at the pharmacy?
What would you say at the next update if you had no answer?
How would you follow up after the fix?

prompt: Exercise: in three sentences, explain to a pharmacy manager why a connection between our software and their system failed overnight. Use no jargon.
variants: Explain a technical failure to a non-technical customer.
intent: Tests translation under constraint: the manager needs impact, cause in plain words, and what happens next.
answerGuide: Sentence one: what they experienced and what is working now.
Sentence two: the cause by analogy (two systems that talk lost their agreed way of identifying each other after a change) without acronyms.
Sentence three: what you are doing and when you will update them, plus anything they need to do.
Avoid blaming them or a third party and avoid false certainty.
followUps: How would you explain it to a pharmacist on shift?
How do you check they understood?
Would you change anything for an email versus a call?

prompt: How do you decide which knowledge base articles to write, and how do you know an article works?
variants: You cut ticket volume. How did you measure that?
intent: Defends your headline metric: whether you can describe cause, measurement and caveats of the 35 percent drop in ticket inflow without overclaiming.
answerGuide: Start from ticket data: top how-to categories by volume and repeat contacts, so articles target real questions.
Write task-based articles with screenshots, link them in replies and in the product where possible.
Measure: ticket inflow for those categories before and after, article views, deflection (viewed then did not contact), and reopen rates.
Be honest about confounders such as seasonality, product changes, or customer mix.
pitfalls: Presenting 35 percent as purely your work.
followUps: What was the baseline period?
Which categories dropped most?
How would you test whether the articles caused the drop?

prompt: What phases does a software implementation usually have, and what do you deliver in each?
variants: Walk me through an implementation from signed contract to steady state.
intent: Checks you can see the whole sequence, which is what the role owns: discovery, setup, data, training, testing, go-live and handover.
answerGuide: Kickoff and discovery: goals, users, workflows, data sources, success criteria and a plan with dates.
Configuration and data import: set up roles, rules and sample data, then migrate real data.
Testing and training: customer UAT, role-based training, and a go-live checklist.
Go-live, hypercare, and handover to support with a review of the success criteria.
followUps: Which phase most often slips?
What do you do when discovery reveals a surprise?
How do you set the timeline?

prompt: What do you cover in a customer kickoff call, and what do you want to have agreed by the end?
variants: How do you run the first meeting with a new customer?
intent: Kickoff sets expectations for the whole project; the interviewer checks whether yours leaves with owners, dates and success measures.
answerGuide: Introductions and roles on both sides, goals in the customer's words, scope in and out, timeline, and what you need from them with dates.
Agree communication rhythm, escalation paths and how decisions are made.
Agree what success looks like and how it will be measured.
Send written notes the same day.
pitfalls: A sales-style presentation with no agreements.
followUps: What if the sponsor is absent?
How do you handle an unrealistic date?
What goes in the follow-up note?

prompt: What is the difference between configuring software and customising it, and why does it matter to a customer?
variants: How do you decide what to say yes to in an implementation?
intent: Tests judgement on scope: configuration is supported and upgrade-safe, customisation creates cost and risk.
answerGuide: Configuration uses settings the product provides (roles, templates, rules); customisation changes behaviour with new development.
Customisation adds time, cost, testing effort and upgrade risk, and needs sign-off and ownership.
Default to configuration, log customer requests as feature requests with evidence, and escalate custom work to product or sales with an impact estimate.
Explain it to the customer in terms of outcomes and risk.
pitfalls: Agreeing to custom changes to keep the customer happy.
followUps: What would you say to a customer who insists?
Who prices custom work?
How do you record a deviation?

prompt: How would you set up user roles and permissions for a new customer, and what can go wrong?
variants: What do you check when a user cannot see something they should?
intent: Access errors are a top onboarding issue and a privacy risk; this checks least-privilege thinking and a method for access complaints.
answerGuide: Gather the customer's job roles and what each needs to see and do, and map them to the product's roles.
Use least privilege: give the minimum, add on request, and review periodically.
Test by logging in as or simulating each role before go-live.
For a missing view, check role, assignment to the location or account, and any filters before assuming a bug.
pitfalls: Giving everyone admin to avoid tickets.
followUps: How do you handle a departing employee?
How do you handle a request for broad access?
What would you document?

prompt: What is hypercare after go-live and how would you run the first two weeks?
variants: What do you do after a customer goes live?
intent: Checks that you plan for the risky first weeks: fast response, early adoption checks and a clean handover.
answerGuide: Heightened support with a named contact, fast response targets and a daily check-in at first.
Watch usage and data quality (who has logged in, what is stuck) and catch confusion before it becomes tickets.
Record issues and patterns, fix quick wins, and feed product issues to the right team.
Close with a handover to standard support and a success review against the goals.
followUps: How do you know hypercare can end?
What if the customer treats you as their permanent helpdesk?
How do you report it?

prompt: A customer sends their staff list as a messy spreadsheet to import. How do you prepare and validate it?
variants: How do you import customer data safely?
intent: A concrete implementation task: graders look for a template, cleaning rules, a test load and reconciliation, not a blind import.
answerGuide: Provide a template with required fields and examples, and agree how to treat duplicates, blanks and formats (dates, phone numbers, licence numbers).
Clean and flag issues in a copy; return a list of questions to the customer instead of guessing.
Load a small sample into a test environment, check results against the source, then run the full load.
Reconcile counts and spot-check records afterwards, keep the original file, and plan how to undo the load.
pitfalls: Fixing data silently without telling the customer.
followUps: What if 5 percent of rows fail?
How would you check duplicates with SQL?
Who signs off the migrated data?

prompt: Exercise: a pharmacy group with 12 stores signs on Monday and wants to be live in three weeks. Outline your onboarding plan and the first three questions you ask.
variants: Plan an onboarding for a fast-moving customer.
intent: A practical scenario: graders look for realistic phasing, early risk spotting and questions about data, users and deadlines.
answerGuide: Questions: what drives the three-week date, who are the users and roles per store, and where do their shift and staff data live today.
Plan: week one discovery, setup and data load for a pilot store; week two pilot with UAT and training; week three roll out in waves with hypercare.
Call out risks: data quality, availability of store managers, training time, and the dependency on their decisions.
State what you would drop or push if the date cannot move.
pitfalls: Agreeing to all 12 stores at once without a pilot.
No mention of the customer's tasks.
followUps: What if the customer wants all stores in week two?
How would you train 12 managers?
What would make you push back on the date?

prompt: Explain what a pivot table and VLOOKUP do, and give an example from your work.
variants: How strong are you in Excel?
intent: States your real Excel level (pivot tables and VLOOKUP, moderate) and checks you can explain, not just use, those tools.
answerGuide: A pivot table summarises rows by categories, such as shifts filled by pharmacy by month, and can be rearranged by dragging fields.

VLOOKUP finds a value in the first column of a table and returns a value from another column, useful for adding pharmacy names to a list of ids; mention exact-match mode and its limitation that the key must be on the left.
Give one real example with the result it produced.
Say honestly you did not write macros or VBA, and that you are learning newer functions such as XLOOKUP.
followUps: What happens if the lookup key has trailing spaces?
How would you do this in SQL instead?
What would you check before sharing the pivot?

prompt: You get an export with 20,000 rows. Before building anything, how do you check it in Excel?
variants: What data issues do you look for first?
intent: Operations and data roles start with suspect data; this checks a systematic first pass and awareness of common traps.
answerGuide: Row count against the source, header meaning, and date formats stored as text.
Duplicates on the key, blanks in required columns, inconsistent spellings or trailing spaces, and impossible values such as a fill time before the request.
Sort and filter extremes, and compare totals with a figure from the source system.
Keep the raw sheet untouched and make changes on a copy with notes.
followUps: How would you deal with duplicates safely?
What if two sources disagree?
When would you stop using Excel and ask for SQL?

prompt: How do you write a standard operating procedure so a new person can follow it without asking you?
variants: How do you document a repeatable process?
intent: Checks writing discipline for process work: purpose, steps, exceptions and a test with a real reader.
answerGuide: State the purpose, trigger, owner and tools needed.
Numbered steps with one action each, screenshots where needed, and the expected result of each step.
Include exceptions and who to ask, and a revision date.
Test it by watching someone new follow it and fix where they stall.
pitfalls: Writing it from memory and never testing.
followUps: How do you keep it current?
When is a checklist better than an SOP?
How would you handle a step that varies by customer?

prompt: You are asked to build a weekly operations dashboard. How do you decide what goes on it?
variants: What makes a dashboard useful rather than decorative?
intent: Tests judgement about audience and decisions; honest about Power BI being new while showing the thinking transfers.
answerGuide: Start from the decisions and the reader: what will they do differently if a number changes.
Pick a few headline measures with definitions, comparisons (last week, target) and one drill-down, not twenty charts.
Add data freshness and definitions on the page so numbers are trusted.
Be honest that at work you built this kind of reporting in SQL and Excel, and that you are learning Power BI on your own.
followUps: How would you validate the dashboard?
Who owns the definitions?
What would you drop if space were short?

prompt: Two teams report different cancellation rates for the same month. How do you find out why?
variants: How do you reconcile conflicting definitions of a metric?
intent: A realistic reporting problem: most mismatches come from definitions and filters, and an analyst should check those before the data.
answerGuide: Compare the formulas: numerator, denominator, which statuses and date field, time zone, and whether emergency or test records are included.
Rerun both from the same source and see where the row sets diverge.
Explain the difference in writing, propose one agreed definition, and name an owner.
Avoid declaring one team wrong until you have proven it.
followUps: Which difference is most common in your experience?
How would you document the definition?
What if both are valid for different uses?

prompt: A queue gets 200 requests a day and each takes 12 minutes. How many people do you need, and what else matters?
variants: How do you estimate staffing for an operational process?
intent: A small numerical case question: arithmetic, then real-world judgement about utilisation and variability.
answerGuide: 200 x 12 minutes = 2,400 minutes, or 40 hours of work a day; with roughly 6 productive hours per person that is about 7 people.
Add allowances: breaks, training, absence, and spikes (peak hours, month-end).
Ask what response-time target applies, since a tight service level needs spare capacity.
Suggest tracking actual handling time rather than the estimate and revisit after a month.
pitfalls: Presenting one number with false precision.
followUps: What if volume doubles at month-end?
What would you automate first?
How would you validate the 12 minutes?

prompt: Exercise: the weekly report says 412 shifts were completed, but the manager's count shows 398. You have 30 minutes before the review. What do you do?
variants: A report's numbers do not match another source. How do you handle it?
intent: A staple operations case: graders check order of work (definitions, filters, timing) and honest communication if you cannot close the gap in time.
answerGuide: Ask how the manager counted, then compare definitions and date ranges (completed by start date or by completion time, time zone, test data, cancelled-after-start).
Query the underlying records and list the 14 differing shifts, then categorise why they differ.
Tell the meeting owner early what you have, how confident you are, and what remains unexplained.
Fix the cause for next week: a documented definition and an automated check.
pitfalls: Presenting the report without mentioning the discrepancy.
followUps: What if you cannot explain it before the meeting?
Which number would you present?
How do you prevent recurrence?

prompt: Exercise: weekly fill rate dropped from 91 to 84 percent. Write the three-sentence note you send to leadership, assuming you have only found part of the cause.
variants: Summarise a metric drop for executives with incomplete information.
intent: Tests concise, honest analytic writing: size of change, probable drivers, certainty level and next step.
answerGuide: Sentence one states the change and its size, with comparison period.
Sentence two gives what you found so far (for example, the drop is concentrated in emergency requests in two regions) and marks it as partial.
Sentence three names the next check and when you will update, plus any decision needed.
No speculation presented as fact.
pitfalls: Hedging so much that nothing is said.
Blaming a cause with no evidence.
followUps: How would you check the cause?
What would you do if leadership demands a cause now?
What would you add for a chart?

prompt: What happens with NULL in a WHERE clause or an average, and how do you handle it?
variants: Why did my count change when I added a filter on a nullable column?
intent: Probes a classic source of wrong numbers; interviewers use it to separate memorised syntax from understanding.
answerGuide: NULL means unknown, so comparisons with = or <> do not match; use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL.
Aggregates such as AVG and COUNT(column) skip NULL values, while COUNT(*) counts rows.
Example: filled_at is NULL for open shifts, so average time to fill silently excludes them, which must be said in the report.
COALESCE can substitute a value when the business rule allows it.
pitfalls: Treating NULL as zero or empty text.
Not stating which rows an average excluded.
followUps: How would you count open shifts?
What does a LEFT JOIN do with NULL?
When would COALESCE be wrong?

prompt: Your query joins shifts to assignments and the total shift count goes up. What happened and how do you fix it?
variants: How do you detect a join that multiplied rows?
intent: Checks the number-one intermediate SQL bug: a one-to-many join inflating counts.
answerGuide: A shift with more than one assignment row appears once for each, so counts multiply.
Check by comparing COUNT(*) with COUNT(DISTINCT shift id) and by looking at one id's rows.
Fix by deduplicating first (a subquery or CTE picking the latest assignment), aggregating before joining, or counting distinct ids with a stated reason.
Verify against a known figure.
pitfalls: Adding DISTINCT blindly to make the number look right.
Not checking row counts after a join.
followUps: When is COUNT DISTINCT misleading?
How would you pick the latest assignment?
How do you test a query like this?

prompt: How would you compute average time to fill a shift, and what decisions do you have to make?
variants: Write the logic for time to fill in SQL.
intent: A domain-specific analysis question: the code is easy, the definitions are the test.
answerGuide: Time to fill is the gap between request time and filled time for shifts that were filled, using the right date functions for the database.
Decisions: exclude open and cancelled shifts and say so, treat emergency and planned shifts separately, choose mean or median since a few long fills skew the average.
Check for impossible values such as negative durations.
Group by month so a trend is visible.
pitfalls: Averaging over all rows including unfilled ones.
followUps: Mean or median, and why?
How do you handle shifts filled twice?
How would you chart it?

prompt: When would you use a CTE instead of a subquery, and have you used window functions?
variants: How do you structure a long SQL query?
intent: Tests readable-query habits and honesty about depth; window functions are a common next-level probe.
answerGuide: A CTE names an intermediate result so the query reads top to bottom; useful when the step is reused or complex.
Subqueries are fine for small, one-off needs.
Window functions compute things like row number or running totals without collapsing rows; say honestly whether you have used them and describe the level.
Mention testing each step on its own.
pitfalls: Claiming performance claims you did not test.
followUps: How would you get the latest assignment per pharmacist?
How do you debug a long query?
What would you check for performance?

prompt: What do accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness and uniqueness mean for data, and how would you test each in a shifts table?
variants: How do you check data quality?
intent: A standard data operations question; the answer should be concrete tests, not definitions alone.
answerGuide: Accuracy: values match reality, tested by sampling against a trusted source.
Completeness: required fields are filled, such as a cancel reason on cancelled shifts.
Consistency: same fact agrees across tables; Timeliness: data arrives when needed; Uniqueness: no duplicate records for one shift.
Show a check for each (count of nulls, mismatched statuses, filled_at before requested_at) and how you would report results.
pitfalls: Treating data quality as a one-time clean.
followUps: Which would you automate first?
What would you do with a failing check?
Who owns fixing source data?

prompt: You must load a daily CSV from a partner into a table. What checks run before and after the load?
variants: How would you build checks around a data feed?
intent: Tests operational discipline on a feed: expected structure, volumes, and what happens on failure.
answerGuide: Before: file received on time, expected columns and types, row count within a normal range, no duplicate keys.
Load into a staging table first, apply rules, and reject bad rows with reasons.
After: reconcile counts and totals to the file, alert on failure, and keep the raw file.
Say plainly that you have done this style of check in SQL and spreadsheets rather than a formal pipeline tool.
pitfalls: Loading straight to the final table.
followUps: What if the file is late?
What if volumes drop by half?
How do you tell the partner?

prompt: You are working with a dataset that has names and licence numbers. How do you handle it?
variants: How do you protect sensitive data in analysis?
intent: Checks privacy habits that matter in healthcare-adjacent data work before the first real dataset is handed over.
answerGuide: Use the minimum necessary: drop or mask identifiers you do not need.
Share only through approved systems, avoid emailing extracts, and never paste data into unapproved tools including AI chat tools.
Store in access-controlled locations and delete working copies when done.
Ask the data owner what rules apply when unsure.
pitfalls: Pasting real records into a public AI tool.
followUps: What would you do if you spotted a record shared too widely?
How would you create a safe practice set?
Who do you tell about a mistake?

prompt: Explain ETL and where it might fit in a reporting setup. Have you built pipelines?
variants: What is the difference between ETL and ELT?
intent: Conceptual literacy question; your honest answer is that you use SQL for retrieval and reporting and have not built production pipelines.
answerGuide: ETL extracts data from sources, transforms it (clean, join, reshape) and loads it to a reporting store; ELT loads first and transforms inside the database.
Link to reporting: a scheduled process feeds a table that reports read from, so everyone sees the same numbers.
State plainly that you used SQL and exports for reporting and did not build or maintain pipelines.
Say you would learn the team's tooling.
followUps: Where would you validate the data?
What is a staging table?
What would you want to learn first?

prompt: Exercise: using shifts(id, pharmacy_id, requested_at, status, cancel_reason), write a query for the monthly cancellation rate and the share of cancellations by reason. Explain your choices.
variants: Write and explain a query for cancellation rate by month.
intent: A live SQL exercise: graders mark the correct grouping and denominator, readable code, and your statement of assumptions.
answerGuide: Group by month of requested_at, count cancelled shifts divided by all shifts (decide whether open shifts count) using a decimal division.
A second query or a grouped breakdown by cancel_reason restricted to cancelled shifts.
State assumptions: which date defines the month, how NULL reasons are shown.
Sanity check: reasons sum to the cancelled total, rate between 0 and 100.
pitfalls: Using the wrong denominator without saying so.
followUps: How do you handle a month with no shifts?
How would you show this by pharmacy?
How would you check the result?

prompt: What is time to value and how would you shorten it for a new customer?
variants: How do you make sure a new customer gets value quickly?
intent: Customer success hiring screens for the first-90-days instinct: define value early and remove blockers.
answerGuide: Time to value is the time from signing to the customer's first meaningful outcome, for example their first emergency shift filled.
Agree that outcome up front, then plan the shortest path: setup, data, training for the first users.
Remove friction: templates, pre-filled configuration, concise guides, and a scheduled check on day 7 and day 30.
Track adoption signals and intervene when a milestone slips.
followUps: What if the customer champion is too busy?
What would a day-30 check look at?
How do you measure it?

prompt: A customer's logins fell 40 percent over two months and renewal is in 90 days. What is your plan?
variants: How do you handle an at-risk account in an async model?
intent: Tests structured risk response: diagnose, reach out through the right people, fix the cause, and track recovery.
answerGuide: Diagnose from data: which users stopped, which features, any recent tickets, change of staff or process.
Reach out to the champion with a specific observation and an offer (a short session, a refresher), not a generic check-in.
Find the real reason: staffing change, missing capability, a bug, or low value; plan a fix with dates.
Track recovery weekly and escalate internally if product issues are the cause.
pitfalls: Waiting for renewal to raise it.
followUps: What if the champion left?
What if they say they will cancel?
What data would you pull first?

prompt: How would you build a simple customer health score, and what would make you distrust it?
variants: What goes into customer health?
intent: Tests data thinking in customer roles: signals tied to outcomes, simple weights and validation.
answerGuide: Choose signals tied to retention: active users, usage of key features, ticket volume and severity, survey scores, and engagement with the team.
Combine with simple weights into green, amber, red and validate against customers who left or renewed.
Distrust it when it contradicts what account notes say, or when signals are lagging.
Review it with the people who know the customers.
pitfalls: A complicated score nobody can explain.
followUps: How would you validate it?
Who would own it?
What would you do with an amber account?

prompt: In an async customer success role, how do you keep many customers informed and still feel personal?
variants: How do you build relationships without live calls?
intent: Probes written-communication craft and systems for a remote, low-touch model, which is how the target roles run.
answerGuide: Use short written updates with the ask at the top, recorded walkthroughs or screenshots, and a predictable rhythm.
Keep a simple record per account of goals, people and open issues so notes are specific.
Offer a call when text is failing (a disagreement, a complex change) and move back to writing with a summary.
Set response expectations and meet them.
followUps: How do you read a customer's mood in text?
What do you do when you get no reply?
How do you handle time zones?

prompt: A strategic customer asks you to promise a feature by quarter end. What do you say?
variants: How do you handle roadmap questions from customers?
intent: Tests whether you stay honest about commitments while preserving the relationship.
answerGuide: Understand the need and the business reason behind the date.
Do not commit what you do not control; share what is planned, what is not, and the confidence level, after checking with product.
Offer interim options: a workaround, a manual process, or early access if available.
Record the request with evidence and update the customer when it changes.
followUps: What if sales already promised it?
How do you involve product?
What if they threaten to leave?

prompt: How do you suggest additional features or seats to a customer without sounding like a salesperson?
variants: How do you feel about upselling?
intent: Customer success roles often carry a revenue component; the interviewer checks you can do it honestly and tied to the customer's goals.
answerGuide: Lead with the customer's goals and data: where a gap is costing them, then show how an addition solves it.
Be willing to say a purchase is not needed.
Bring in the account executive for pricing and contracts.
Measure by outcomes the customer cares about, not by pushing volume.
pitfalls: Pitching features unrelated to their needs.
Pretending you are not allowed to talk about it.
followUps: Have you ever advised against a purchase?
How do you handle a customer who is suspicious?
How would you track expansion?

prompt: What does 'minimum necessary' mean, and how does it change what you share in an email or ticket?
variants: How much patient information should you include when escalating an issue?
intent: Tests practical privacy habits rather than HIPAA trivia: what a careful coordinator puts in writing.
answerGuide: Share only what the recipient needs to do their task, with identifiers masked or replaced by record ids when possible.
Use approved systems for anything sensitive and avoid free-text detail in tickets and chats.
Check recipients before sending; use the organisation's secure messaging rather than personal tools.
Be honest that your background is software and operations rather than a patient-records role; the habit is the same.
pitfalls: Claiming certification you do not hold.
followUps: What would you do if a ticket contained a full record?
How would you handle a request from someone you cannot verify?
Where do you ask when unsure?

prompt: You realise you sent a schedule containing patient names to the wrong external address. What do you do, in order?
variants: How do you respond to a privacy incident you caused?
intent: Probes incident honesty and speed: report immediately through the proper route, do not try to quietly fix it.
answerGuide: Stop further sharing, try to recall the message if the system allows, and note exactly what was sent and to whom.
Report to your supervisor and the privacy or compliance contact at once, following the organisation's procedure.
Cooperate with assessment and any notification decision, which is made by the responsible team.
Afterwards, add a check such as address confirmation or secure-mail rules.
pitfalls: Deciding by yourself that it is harmless.
followUps: Why report even if the risk seems low?
What would you add to prevent it?
How would you tell the person affected, if it were your job?

prompt: When assigning a contracted pharmacist to a pharmacy, why do licence and state details matter, and how would you check them?
variants: How do you make sure staff are eligible to work a shift?
intent: Ties your actual product domain (dispatching licensed pharmacists) to the compliance mindset healthcare admin teams want.
answerGuide: A pharmacist generally must hold a valid licence in the state where the pharmacy operates; an invalid or expired licence is a legal and safety risk.
Verify against the licensing authority's records or the organisation's verified credential file, check expiry dates, and record who verified and when.
Block assignment automatically where possible and flag exceptions for human review.
Be careful not to state specific legal rules you are unsure of; say you would follow the compliance team's policy.
pitfalls: Treating verification as a one-time step.
followUps: What if the licence expires tomorrow?
What if the database and the pharmacist disagree?
How do you handle a multi-state licence?

prompt: Three pharmacies request emergency coverage for the same evening and you have two available pharmacists. How do you decide?
variants: How do you prioritise urgent staffing gaps?
intent: Domain scenario drawn from emergency staffing: tests criteria, transparency and escalation rather than a single 'right' answer.
answerGuide: Clarify the facts for each: opening hours at risk, whether another pharmacy is nearby, patient-impact (critical medications, emergency room supply), and contractual priorities.
Apply the organisation's published triage rules if any; if none, escalate the decision quickly with a recommendation and rationale.
Tell all three requesters what is happening and when they will hear back; look for alternatives (later shift, floater, another pool).
Document the decision.
followUps: What if one is a long-standing customer?
What would you change in the process?
How would you record the outcome?

prompt: How do you explain a policy or delay to a patient or pharmacy staff member in plain language?
variants: How do you communicate with people who are stressed or in a hurry?
intent: Checks calm, short, accurate communication for people who cannot absorb detail under stress.
answerGuide: Put the most important information first, in short sentences without internal terms.
Acknowledge the situation, say what you can do, and what you cannot, with the reason in one line.
Confirm understanding by asking them to restate the next step.
Follow up in writing when accuracy matters.
followUps: What if they want clinical advice?
What would you say to a caller who is shouting?
How do you communicate delays by message?

prompt: Why does an audit trail matter in healthcare administration, and how do you keep one when you change a record?
variants: How do you document corrections to a record?
intent: Probes record-keeping habits that matter in regulated settings: who changed what, when and why.
answerGuide: An audit trail shows who made a change, when, and why, which supports accountability, investigations and trust.
Never overwrite silently: correct through the approved process, note the reason and keep the original value visible where policy requires it.
Use the system's change logs, and add a note referencing the request or ticket.
Escalate if you find an unexplained change.
pitfalls: Editing records directly with no note.
Not knowing who may authorise a change.
followUps: Give an example of a correction you handled.
What if a coworker asks you to change a time stamp?
Where would you look for history?

prompt: What is a near miss, and why should an administrator report one?
variants: Tell me how you would handle an almost-error.
intent: Tests safety culture: reporting small errors is how healthcare organisations prevent large ones.
answerGuide: A near miss is an error caught before harm, such as a wrong shift time noticed before the pharmacist travelled.
Report it promptly through the proper system, describing facts without blame.
Explain the value: patterns show process weaknesses, such as an unclear form or confusing screen.
Say how you would follow up: a checklist, a validation rule, or a training note.
followUps: What is the difference between a near miss and an incident?
Have you reported one?
How would you encourage reporting on a team?

prompt: A scheduling system shows a pharmacist booked at two locations at overlapping times. How do you handle it?
variants: What do you do when the schedule conflicts?
intent: A direct scheduling problem in healthcare staffing: quick fix for the day, investigation of the cause and communication to both locations.
answerGuide: Confirm the conflict with the source record and contact the pharmacist and the scheduler.
Decide which assignment stands using the rules or the requester's priority, and arrange cover for the other; tell both pharmacies promptly.
Investigate the cause: a manual override, a race between two dispatchers, or a missing validation.
Raise a defect or process fix with evidence, and check for other overlaps.
pitfalls: Fixing the single case and ignoring the cause.
followUps: How would you detect overlaps with SQL?
How would you test the fix?
What if the pharmacist already accepted both?

prompt: Exercise: an email arrives from someone claiming to be a patient's daughter asking which pharmacist worked her father's prescription yesterday. Write your reply and your next steps.
variants: Draft a response to a request for protected information from an unverified person.
intent: A realistic admin exercise: graders look for politeness, no disclosure, a verified route, and escalation.
answerGuide: Reply politely without confirming or denying any record exists or sharing any detail.
Explain the proper route: the patient or an authorised representative can contact the pharmacy directly or use the official request process.
Do not add identifiers or details in your reply.
Tell your supervisor or the privacy contact and log the request.
pitfalls: Giving a name to be helpful.
Writing a cold reply that blames them.
followUps: What if she is upset and says it is urgent?
How would you verify identity?
Would you log the email, and where?
